extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Indian poetics, dramaturgy, and literary theory; creative-writing researchers interested in classical aesthetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Bharata's Natyashastra-based rasa theory for analysis or creation of dramatic and poetic works, including the bhava/rasa taxonomy, mechanisms of rasa production, representation modes, and spectator-specific conditions. Useful for literary criticism, dramaturgy, and creative-writing grounded in classical Indian aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibhavanubhav-vyabhicharibhav-samyogadrasanispattih (Bharata's rasa sutra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's aphorism summarizing the process of rasa: the conjunction (samyoga) of vibhav, anubhav and vyabhicharibhav leads to rasa-nispatti (manifestation of rasa). (Natyashastra, VI)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as the core process: a proper combination/correlation of excitants (vibhav), ensuing responses (anubhav) and transitory feelings (sancharibhav/vyabhicharibhav) with a sthayibhav in the perceiver produces aesthetic pleasure (rasa). Used as the central explanatory mechanism (example: Karuna/compassion illustrated by death + mourning + transitory reactions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sthayibhav (permanent emotion / dominant sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sthayibhav is an inborn, permanent emotion that forms the central, enduring affective core (e.g., love, mirth, grief, anger, enthusiasm, fear, disgust, surprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rasa is grounded in a sthayibhav; the sthayibhav 'transforms into' rasa when properly evoked. Bharata enumerates eight primary sthayibhav (some later commentators add more). Sthayibhav is like the 'king' to which transitory feelings are subordinate and is necessary for sustained aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sancharibhav / Vyabhicharibhav (transitory/auxiliary feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sancharibhav are fleeting, changeable feelings that arise in the course of action and are subordinate to sthayibhav (examples: bashfulness, trembling, longing, recollection, agitation, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as roughly thirty transitory emotions; they are neither inborn nor permanent but arise from or accompany sthayibhav. They diversify the manifestation of a sthayibhav and are necessary as accessory feelings in the rasa-forming process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sattvikbhav (involuntary bodily responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sattvikbhav are involuntary physiological/bodily responses (e.g., paralysis, fainting, horripilation, perspiration, tears, change of color, trembling, change/breaking of voice) that indicate deep emotional stirring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although less discussed, sattvikbhav play a significant role in signaling intense bhava; in performance these are part of abhinaya and help the spectator perceive the underlying sthayibhav and thereby the rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibhav (excitant causes: alambana and uddipana)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibhav are the determinants or causes that generate a bhava when presented: Alambana vibhav (substantial/objects/subjects, e.g., the lover and beloved) and Uddipana vibhav (external enhancers/background, e.g., season, moonlight, scenery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vibhav are directly graspable by the senses and act as the objective-correlative that triggers bhava and subsequent anubhav; for effective rasa-creation a work must present appropriate alambana and uddipana vibhav.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anubhav (ensuing responses/effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anubhav are the expressive consequences or observable responses that follow a bhava (e.g., tears and lamentation in karuna; exclamation and wide eyes in adbhuta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anubhav are what can be perceived by the senses as the effect of bhava; they, together with vibhav and sancharibhav, indicate and lead to the manifestation of rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sadharanikaran (universalization/generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory that particular, individual details presented in art are transformed into general/universal forms so the spectator can experience rasa without personal prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bhattanayaka/Abhinavgupta's account: through Sadharanikaran the spectator's mind is freed from individuality and prejudices, allowing sthayibhav to mature into rasa. It is operationalized via three functions of words (shabda-vyapara): abhidha-vyapara (conventional meaning), bhavaktva-vyapara (generalization of vibhav/anubhav/sancharibhav), and bhoj-vyapara/bhog-vyapara (the resultant enjoyment). Key summary points: (1) transform particular into general; (2) universalize action; (3) free spectator from prejudices; (4) foregrounding supports rasa; (5) sthayibhav matures when correlated with generalized bhavas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of words (abhidha-vyapara, bhavaktva-vyapara, bhoj/bhog-vyapara)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three linguistic/psychological functions required for universalization and enjoyment: abhidha-vyapara (conventional meaning/arousal of images), bhavaktva-vyapara (making the vibhav/anubhav/sancharibhav generalizable), bhoj-vyapara (the enjoyment state—bhog—experienced by the spectator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These functions explain how language and representation convert individual particulars into universalized stimuli enabling rasa; critics/creators should ensure that words and presentation accomplish these three functions for successful aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Rasa (Bharata's eight; Abhinavgupta's shanta addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's canonical rasas: Sringara (erotic), Hasya (comic), Karuna (compassionate), Rudra (furious/horror), Vira (heroic), Bhayanak (terrifying/fear), Bibhatsa (disgust), Adbhuta (wonder/awesome). Abhinavgupta later added Shanta (peace) as a ninth rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each rasa corresponds to a sthayibhav and has characteristic vibhav, anubhav and sancharibhav. Bharata insists the aim of art is pleasure; rasas are pleasurable even when derived from tragic emotions. Creators should design incidents/abhinaya to elicit the appropriate combination of determinants for the intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sringara Rasa (erotic) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Sringara arises from the sthayibhav of love; associated with what is bright, pure, beautiful. Alambana vibhav: young noble lovers; Uddipana vibhav: seasons, garlands, ornaments; Anubhav: coy glances, sweet words; Sancharibhav: jealousy, suspicion, affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke Sringara, present appropriate lovers/objects and enhancing background; use suggestive diction and abhinaya (gestures, looks) to produce the pertinent anubhav and transitory feelings so the spectator's sthayibhav of love can mature into rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasya Rasa (humor/comic) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasya arises from a joyous permanent affect; vibhav may be peculiarity of dress/speech; anubhav includes spouting, mimicking; sancharibhav: smile, snicker, laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect depends on character peculiarities and audience recognition; timing and representation (abhinaya) must make the excitants and ensuing responses perceptible and generalized so spectator experiences bhog (enjoyment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Karuna Rasa (compassion/tragedy) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Karuna arises from the sthayibhav of sorrow/grief; vibhav include loss, death, calamity; anubhav: tears, fainting, lamentation; sancharibhav: sorrow, trembling, fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict believable excitants and natural ensuing responses; sattvik and anubhava must convincingly indicate grief so the spectator's sthayibhav of sorrow can be evoked and then universalized into rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudra Rasa (fury/horror) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudra arises from sthayibhav related to anger/violence; vibhav: anger, violence, treachery; anubhav: red eyes, rubbing hands, biting lips; sancharibhav: sweating, impatience, excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray forceful excitants and visceral anubhav; use sattvik signs and acting intensity to produce the sense of fury without harming the spectator's pleasure (art should give pleasure even when depicting violent emotions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vira Rasa (heroic) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Vira arises from the sthayibhav of determination/valor; vibhav: strength, bravery; anubhav: courageous acts, generosity; sancharibhav: resoluteness, arrogance/decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroic rasa requires depiction of noble deeds and consequent responses; staging, diction and action should foreground courage and resolve, enabling spectators to experience generalized admiration and bhog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhayanak Rasa (fear/terrifying) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhayanak arises from sthayibhav of fear; vibhav: frightful sights, darkness, lonely places; anubhav: trembling, pallor, loss of voice; sancharibhav: fainting, hurrying, being rooted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evoke environmental and action-based excitants plus convincing anubhav to trigger fear in a generalized, aesthetically pleasurable way (often through suggestion rather than graphic realism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibhatsa Rasa (disgust) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibhatsa arises from sthayibhav of disgust/nausea; vibhav: repulsive news/sights; anubhav: spitting, turning up nose; sancharibhav: fainting, sickness, hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disgust can be evoked through appropriate sensory details; creators must balance representation so disgust is aestheticized (pleasurable in an aesthetic context) rather than purely repellent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adbhuta Rasa (wonder/astonishment) — criteria and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Adbhuta arises from sthayibhav of wonder; vibhav: unusual phenomena, miracles, achieving desire; anubhav: wide eyes, thrill, exclamation; sancharibhav: standing stunned, over-joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict novel or surprising excitants and ensure the spectator perceives the natural anubhav; wonder is often produced by staged revelation, magical elements or unexpected competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of art: aesthetic pleasure (rasa) and non-harm to spectator
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata asserts the aim of art is pleasure: the rasa contained should give pleasure and 'should not hurt the spectator.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic choices (plot, depiction of violence, tragic material) should be arranged to produce aesthetic delight (rasa) rather than causing real distress; even negative emotions are aestheticized into pleasurable rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sadharanikaran operational summary (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical corollaries of Sadharanikaran for creators: (1) transform particular into general; (2) universalize the whole action during rasa manifestation; (3) free the spectator from prejudices; (4) foreground universalized elements to realize poetic pleasure; (5) correlate sthayibhav with other bhavas to mature rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language, representation and staging that abstracts individuality (space/time) so spectator can identify with generalized human states; ensure the three shabda-vyaparas occur in sequence to produce enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation modes: Lokadharmi (realistic) vs Natyadharmi (codified/symbolic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata distinguishes two types of representation: Lokdharmi (realistic representation) and Natyadharmi (symbolical/codified representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators choose mode depending on the work: Natyadharmi supports universalized abhinaya and codified signs (suits rasa theory), whereas Lokadharmi aims for realism; Bharata often privileges natyadharmi for manifestation of rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold acting: Aharya, Angika, Vachik and Sattvik
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's fourfold acting categories: Aharya (costume, make-up, props), Angika (bodily gestures/movement), Vachik (speech/dialogue), and Sattvik (mental/involuntary states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective performance must integrate these four aspects: costuming and stagecraft (aharya), physical acting (angika), verbal expression (vachik), and subtle inner states/sattvik signs to evoke rasa in the spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, alankara, and the guna/dosa distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Natyashastra and commentators emphasize language features: figures of speech (alankara), the qualities (guna) and defects (dosa) of language, and appropriate diction for drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction must be imaginative, suggestive and adorned; mere straightforward statement lacks suggestiveness and cannot be termed creative literature. Use alankara and apt diction to evoke vibhav/anubhav and support rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramaturgy elements: structure, stagecraft, characters, music
rubrics_metrics.description: Natyashastra prescribes comprehensive dramaturgical elements: origin, objectives, theatre structure, stage space (kaksha), methods of representation (dharmi), costumes (pravrti), character types, order of incidents, musical accompaniment (tala, raga), and instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective rasa-evocation, creators and directors must attend to stage design, appropriate costumes/hair, musical structure, scene ordering and character types as specified; these elements function as vibhav/uddipana and contribute to universalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of director/performers and elements of successful representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Natyashastra lists essential qualities for directors and principal artists and enumerates elements of successful representation and causes of dramatic failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directors and performers should possess technical knowledge, craft, sensitivity, and understanding of acting types; attention to balance, mental states of roles, and ensemble coordination determine success; failures often stem from poor representation, inappropriate casting, or technical deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good spectator (sahardya)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata prescribes spectator qualities: no obvious faults, attachment to drama, intact senses, cleverness in inference, capacity to empathize, knowledge of music/dance/acting types and dialects, and refined sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rasa's manifestation depends on spectator capacities; critics and creators should assume or cultivate an audience capable of universalization—sensitive, informed, and open-minded—so that the sthayibhav can mature into rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abhinaya (acting/representation indicates sthayibhav)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abhinaya (performed expression) indicates and manifests sthayibhav through actions, gestures, sattvik signs and verbal expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance, abhinaya must convincingly reflect the sthayibhav and its anubhav/sattvik signs; accurate abhinaya helps spectators recognize vibhav/anubhav and facilitates rasa realization.
